pr_title: Provide alias names for ML-KEM algorithms without dashes
pr_comments: Hmm... unfortunately even with the latest oqs-provider commit the ml-kem tests seem to fail. @baentsch any idea?

The standard has the **"correct"** name for these algorithms - and those are what we should be encouraging people to use. I would suggest that the oqs_provider code needs to get the correct formal names as aliases added if we are going to do this sort of thing - as the names without hyphens aren't following the specification itself. We try to (these days) follow each specifications naming scheme rather than adding our own private format. 

@baentsch are you going to commit to adding compatible names using the names in the standard itself?

IMO OQS ought to support the official names too but that's up to that project's team members.

It seems that Michael is making a valid point, the `TLS-GROUP` capability query result from a provider include various group properties and an algorithm **name**, not a fetched algorithm handle. The algorithm name is resolved in OpenSSL's `t1_lib.c`, using the `libctx` and `propq` of the SSL_CTX resolving the groups, not the provider's `libctx` or `propq`.

I don't see any way for the provider to tell OpenSSL where it would have found the algorithm, if it were to look instead.
To avoid this issue, providers of TLS groups would have to use unique provider-specific aliases for the algorithms associated with their TLS groups for returning to OpenSSL, so that when the algorithm name is resolved it matches the provider's actual algorithm associated with that group.

As it stands, whenever we adopt a common algorithm name, we block the ability of external providers to implement any TLS groups with **their** version of an algorithms sharing the same name... :-(

I think that the capability query should have returned an already fetched algorithm object,rather than a name (**tls-group-alg** property in the docs).  The documentation reads in part:
```
The name of a Key Management algorithm that the provider offers and that should be used with this group.
```
It is not clear that the provider would/should always be the direct source of the algorithm, perhaps it defines the group mapping to an algorithm from a different provider. But for now it may be reasonable to search for the algorithm in the provider that sources the group, and to fetch and save the algorithm, not just its name.

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2457fc4816551a7e982117a4032fd1c259c493a7/ssl/t1_lib.c#L345-L365

> Trying to make `EVP_KEYMGMT_fetch` "get the right thing"? Just tried, but something unsurprising happened: All (connection) tests fail as `oqsprovider` doesn't implement ciphers, RNG etc.

You have to use `?provider=oqsprovider` not `provider=oqsprovider`. This way the oqs provider will be preferred in fetches but not required.

@baentsch Thinking about it - the check whether the provider matches is actually wrong. IMO we can assume that what we get with the same algorithm name, implements the same algorithm as expected, if not, then there is a bigger problem then just mismatching the TLS group support.

> As it stands, whenever we adopt a common algorithm name, we block the ability of external providers to implement any TLS groups with **their** version of an algorithms sharing the same name... :-(

What does **their** version mean. Identical name should imply identical (in terms of the behavior, not implementation) algorithm. Of course that might imply that if somebody decides to implement something completely different under a name mlkem768 than we do, if you load their provider, all hell breaks loose. But that is kind of expected.

> > As it stands, whenever we adopt a common algorithm name, we block the ability of external providers to implement any TLS groups with **their** version of an algorithms sharing the same name... :-(
> 
> What does **their** version mean. Identical name should imply identical (in terms of the behavior, not implementation) algorithm. Of course that might imply that if somebody decides to implement something completely different under a name mlkem768 than we do, if you load their provider, all hell breaks loose. But that is kind of expected.

Sure, the same name should yield mathematically equivalent behaviour, but will the claimed security level or other properties be the same if we load the algorithm from a different provider than intended?

And certainly if we're testing provider implementations of an algorithm, though such testing is certainly not the main concern, then the tests are potentially less meaningful once we have a name collision, FWIW.

> Sure, the same name should yield mathematically equivalent behaviour, but will the claimed security level or other properties be the same if we load the algorithm from a different provider than intended?

Most likely it wouldn't. In the case of `oqsprovider` it definitely doesn't. That's the reason behind [my proposal to remove standard algorithms from oqsprovider](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/discussions/610): That code absolutely does not have the same rigor applied or support available as does `openssl` built-in code. But of course, that's an "external" defense. imo `openssl` also needs a mechanism to protect itself and its users from this. Beyond documentation, I once proposed adding at least an output warning when an algorithm is registered a second time (name, code point, OID, whatever) if not to outright prohibit it (possibly via a new config option like "no-external-standard-algs"). Maybe time to revisit now?

Second rationale: There is a valid reason for enabling a second provider operating the same algorithms, and that is to ascertain it is (functionally) a valid alternative with other non-functional properties (performance, code provenance, marketing/bragging rights, whatever).

I don't think it is practical or desirable to prohibit multiple implementations of the same algorithm name.

Providers that intend their algorithms to be for internal consumption only (e.g. offering a TLS group via an algorithm without intending to export the underlying algorithm) should give their algorithms provider-specific names to avoid conflicts.

Providers that implement an algorithm intended for direct use should give the natural name and let it be resolved based on the usual fetch policy subject to constraints in the property string.

The default provider could perhaps in some cases have reason to also use some private names for algorithms it implements, so as to be reasonably sure to use that version, and not another.

Here "reasonably sure" means when none of the loaded providers are malicious, trying to deliberately override even the private bindings, because once you've loaded code from an untrusted provider the game is over. It makes little sense to attempt to defend against hostile code in the same address space.

> It makes little sense to attempt to defend against hostile code in the same address space.

Sure it doesn't. My suggestion is not targeting defense against "hostile take-over" (that's got to be done --if desired-- at a different level). I'm arguing for defense against "negligent" configs (e.g. driven by marketing desires trumping user interests or plain lack of knowledge).
CI failure due to a missing test restriction. Fix in https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/620.
Latest failure now is more substantial and relates to registering (O|N)IDs for signature algs already registered: See https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/621.

FYI, the problem underlying the CI failure is documented in https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/621. 

Resolving that in turn now hinges on properly [adapting `oqsprovider` to _all_ OpenSSL names](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26328#issuecomment-2574183391) for all algorithms and in all aspects (alg name & TLS name; "-" vs "_"; lowercase vs capital case). As the documentation for those things are not exactly clear to me, the code implementing that (ML-DSA) is not ready yet and I don't want to keep creating code that may be obsolete a week later with the next code update to a feature branch, my preference for addressing that issue thus is only after the dust has settled and at least the feature branch for ML-DSA is feature complete (TLS and X.509 working) such as [to adapt `oqsprovider` fully to that then](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/621#issuecomment-2582765832).

At least until then, my recommendation is to disable `oqsprovider` (just testing, or even building it outright). My _preference_ right now actually is complete removal from the external test harness as the overall OQS software stack is IMO too far behind not just in naming but also (dynamic) key format adaptation ([seed vs extended form](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2032)) such that it now hinders progress in the `openssl` project. Created https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/26386 to discuss/track removal.

Long story short, at the very least for now, @t8m please add "#" in front of https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/b049ce0e354011be075e620b9ba7cf4d7c8f9577/test/recipes/95-test_external_oqsprovider_data/oqsprovider.sh#L76 to land this PR. 

If so OK for you(?), we could track next steps in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/26386.

> I asked for this because we have actual shipping code that understands only the shortened lower-case names (`mklem512`, etc.) in Fedora now (other Linux distributions are available).

That same shipping code in Fedora does not use the NIST defined OIDs nor does it use the updated code to match the final specification. It is at the initial public draft level. It is also by default OCTET wrapping the private key **and** public key rather than just the private key.

I don't think you are suggesting that everyone should support the wrong OIDs and the wrong encoding wrapping and the wrong content going forward simply because test code was shipped in Fedora - or are you actually suggesting that?

Anyone who has generated keys using test OIDs should not be expecting them to be supported **at all** going forward - that is the purpose of having test OIDs - they are for testing - not for production use - and if you put them into a production context then you are creating an obligation on yourself to sort them out down the track. You should not expect future versions of the software to treat test OIDs as aliases.

> That same shipping code in Fedora does not use the NIST defined OIDs nor does it use the updated code to match the final specification. It is at the initial public draft level. It is also by default OCTET wrapping the private key **and** public key rather than just the private key.

Just one nit, yes, the Fedora 41 OQS provider defaults to output test OIDs, but the code for at least ML-KEM does appear to match the final specification.

Sadly, it is shipped with OpenSSL 3.2, which does not support `-encap` or `-decap` in `pkeyutl(1)`. So testing ML-KEM interop required a bit of gymnastics by way of a "neutral" OpenSSL 3.4 build to run `decap` with the `oqsprovider`, and without our new code getting in the way:

doit.sh:
```sh
#! /bin/sh

export PATH=/opt/openssl/3.4/bin:$PATH
export OQS_OID_MLKEM512="2.16.840.1.101.3.4.4.1"

openssl genpkey -provider-path /usr/lib64/ossl-modules \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default \
    -algorithm mlkem512 -out prv-oqs-512.pem

./util/wrap.pl ./apps/openssl pkey \
    -in prv-oqs-512.pem -pubout -out pub-oqs-512.pem 

./util/wrap.pl ./apps/openssl pkeyutl -encap \
    -inkey pub-oqs-512.pem \
    -secret ossl-secret.dat -out ossl-ctext.dat 

openssl pkeyutl -provider-path /usr/lib64/ossl-modules \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default \
    -decap -inkey prv-oqs-512.pem \
    -in ossl-ctext.dat -out oqs-secret.dat

cmp ossl-secret.dat oqs-secret.dat &&
    echo $(wc -c < ossl-secret.dat) bytes match
```
Which, when executed, yields:
```
$ sh ./doit.sh 
32 bytes match
```

issue_context.title: Provide aliases to ML-KEM algorithm names
issue_context.body:
Looking at current feature/ml-kem branch (f60adc4057bbd3), the algorithms have the following names:
- `ML-KEM-512`
- `ML-KEM-768`
- `ML-KEM-1024`

This is in contrast to the names in the [oqs-provider](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider?tab=readme-ov-file#kem-algorithms):
- `mlkem512`
- `mlkem768`
- `mlkem1024`

Those are supposed to be the same algorithms.

Would it be possible to provide aliases to the OpenSSL names that match the oqsprovider names? So that commands like `openssl genpkey -out private-key.pem -algorithm mlkem1024` continue to work?

review_comments: FWIW, I'll also be adding the OID as a string to these in the encoders PR, so whoever is merged last will have to deal with a conflict. But this is not a blocker to approval.
